Business plan text:

Cravemap
Cravemap Executive Summary
Problem
Hospital cafeterias serve a large and captive audience. Nurses, doctors, technicians, patients' families and other visitors all eat there, often several times a week. Many hospitals say they want to promote health, and it looks bad when a hospital cafeteria is mostly fried food and sugary drinks. Despite this, healthy eating in hospital cafeterias is still a challenge. The people who run these cafeterias are under pressure to keep sales up, because cafeterias are expected to cover their costs or even bring in revenue for the hospital. When they try to make the menu healthier, they often do it based on instinct or on a general health guideline, and they do not know what their own customers will actually buy. If a healthy item does not sell, it gets thrown out and the manager becomes more cautious about trying again.
The data to do better exists, since almost every cafeteria has a point of sale system that records every order. But the reports from these systems are basic, hard to use, and not designed for menu decisions. Most managers do not have time or analytics training to dig into them. As a result, the data sits unused and menu changes stay guesswork.
Solution
Cravemap is a mobile analytics service that turns cafeteria sales data into simple, practical guidance for managers. The manager connects Cravemap to the point of sale system, and the app builds dashboards that can be read on a phone in a minute or two. The dashboards show top sellers, slow sellers, busy times of day, and how orders differ between staff and visitors where the data allows it.
The core feature is our menu suggestions. Cravemap looks at what people order and suggests small changes that lean healthier but are unlikely to hurt sales, such as making a salad the default side instead of fries, moving a healthier entree to the top of the menu board, or bundling a fruit cup with a popular sandwich. After a change is made, Cravemap tracks sales before and after so the manager can see whether the change worked. Over time, the system learns which kinds of swaps work in which cafeterias.
Our goal is to give managers confidence that they can improve the healthiness of what they serve without taking a financial risk.
Market
There are thousands of hospitals in the United States, and most of them run some kind of cafeteria, either themselves or through a contracted food service company. We believe the market includes both individual hospitals and the large food service companies that operate cafeterias for many hospitals at once. We have not yet done a detailed market sizing, but a rough estimate is that if there are several thousand hospital cafeterias and each paid a few hundred dollars a month, the market would be in the tens of millions of dollars per year. Over time we could expand to other institutional cafeterias such as universities, corporate campuses, and long term care facilities, which would make the market considerably larger.
Our first target customers are mid-sized hospitals with in-house food service, because decisions can be made quickly there. Food service management companies are a second target because winning one could bring many sites at once.
Business Model
Cravemap will charge a monthly subscription per cafeteria location. We are currently thinking of a basic tier with dashboards and a premium tier that adds menu suggestions and before and after tracking. Pricing has not been finalized, and we expect to adjust it after talking with pilot customers. We are also considering a setup fee for connecting the point of sale system, since integration may take some effort.
Other possible revenue sources include a sponsored placement feature, where food suppliers could promote healthier products to cafeteria managers, and data reports sold to hospital wellness programs. We have not tested either of these ideas and they would need to be handled carefully to keep the trust of our customers.
Competition
There are already many tools in this space. Point of sale vendors offer their own reporting, and general restaurant analytics platforms provide sales insights for restaurants and cafeterias. Nutrition and menu management software exists for institutional food service, mostly focused on compliance and nutrition labeling. Large food service companies also have internal analytics teams. None of these, as far as we can tell, focus specifically on the balance between healthier menus and sales in hospital settings, and none are built mobile first for busy managers. Still, we recognize that a larger competitor could add similar features without much difficulty, so we will need to move quickly and build strong relationships with early customers.
Team
Priya Raghunathan is our chief executive. She studies business and has worked part time in a campus dining operation, where she saw firsthand how little data managers used for decisions. Marcus Delacroix-Webb is our chief technology officer. He studies computer science and built the Cravemap prototype, including the dashboards and the first version of the suggestion logic. Tomasz Kowalczyk leads health and nutrition. He studies public health and is responsible for making sure our menu suggestions are consistent with common nutrition guidelines. We are all students at our university and are working on Cravemap alongside our classes.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core business concept, built a prototype using sample sales data, and registered the company as a C Corp. We have spoken informally with a few people who work in food service, who said the idea sounded useful, but we do not yet have a pilot customer or a signed agreement. We have no revenue. Our spending to date has been small and covered by the founders personally, mostly for incorporation fees and basic software tools.
Over the next twelve months, we plan to recruit one or two pilot hospitals, connect the prototype to real point of sale data, and test whether our menu suggestions can improve the mix of healthier items without reducing sales. If the pilots go well, we would aim to sign our first paying customers in the second half of the year. We expect our main costs to be software development, cloud hosting, and some travel for customer visits. We have not built a detailed financial model yet, and we plan to develop one with feedback from the competition.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to the competition for several reasons. First, we would like funding to support the pilot, including development time and hosting costs for connecting to real data. Second, we would value mentoring from experienced entrepreneurs and from people with healthcare or food service backgrounds, especially help with sales to hospitals, which we understand can be slow. Third, we would appreciate introductions to potential pilot partners and to anyone who can advise us on data privacy and security, since working with hospitals may bring extra requirements. Finally, the competition would give us useful practice presenting our idea and getting honest feedback so we can improve our plan.
Thank you for considering Cravemap. We believe that better data can help hospital cafeterias make healthier food a normal part of the menu, and we are eager to learn and move forward.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.

response.text:
**Viability and Scalability of Business Model and Strategy:**

**1. Viability of Business Model:**
- **Subscription Model:** The proposed monthly subscription model is standard for SaaS products and has proven viable in similar niches. However, the pricing structure is not yet validated. The assumption that "several thousand hospital cafeterias" would pay "a few hundred dollars a month" is optimistic and lacks data support. A more realistic market sizing would be necessary to validate revenue potential.
- **Tiered Pricing:** The basic and premium tiers offer a clear differentiation, but the value proposition for the premium tier (menu suggestions and tracking) needs stronger validation. Pilot testing is essential to determine whether these features justify the additional cost.
- **Alternative Revenue Streams:** Sponsored placements and data reports are potential add-ons, but their viability depends on maintaining customer trust and avoiding perceived conflicts of interest. These features are not yet tested and should be approached cautiously.

**2. Scalability:**
- **Market Potential:** The target market (hospital cafeterias) is large and growing, but the initial focus on mid-sized hospitals with in-house food service is a strategic choice. However, the assumption that food service management companies (which operate for many hospitals) would adopt the product is speculative. Building relationships with these entities will be critical for scaling.
- **Technology Architecture:** The mobile-first, cloud-based approach is scalable, but the integration with point-of-sale systems must be robust and flexible. The current prototype is based on sample data, so real-world integration with diverse POS systems may introduce technical challenges.
- **Data Utilization:** The core value proposition relies on leveraging existing sales data. If the data is not structured or accessible, the product's effectiveness could be limited. The team must address data compatibility and normalization early.

**3. Validity of Assumptions:**
- **Customer Need:** The problem statement is valid—hospital cafeterias struggle with balancing health and sales. However, the assumption that managers lack the time or skills to analyze data is not universally true. Some may have access to analytics tools or have staff with relevant skills.
- **Competitive Differentiation:** The claim that no competitor focuses specifically on the balance between healthier menus and sales in hospital settings is plausible, but it may be difficult to sustain as larger competitors enter the space. The team must differentiate through speed, ease of use, and strong early customer relationships.
- **Team Experience:** The team has relevant skills (business, computer science, public health), but their lack of professional experience in sales, healthcare, or food service may pose a challenge in acquiring early customers and scaling.

**Conclusion:**
Cravemap has a clear and logical business model with a viable path to monetization through a subscription-based service. However, the assumptions about market size, pricing, and customer behavior require further validation. The product has strong potential for scalability, but success will depend on rigorous pilot testing, data integration capabilities, and the ability to differentiate from competitors. The team’s interdisciplinary background is an asset, but they must address gaps in sales experience and market validation to ensure long-term viability.
